opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really fundamental shift. In the traditional software world, product development was very deterministic. You'd write a spec, engineers would build exactly to that spec, you'd test it, and the behavior was predictable. If it didn't work, you'd find the bug and fix it.

With generative AI, the philosophy flips. The core building block, the model, is probabilistic. So application builders can't just design top-down and expect the system to behave exactly as specified. Instead, you have to start from the user experience you want, get something working very quickly, and then iterate relentlessly based on real usage and real data. It's much more empirical, much closer to a scientific loop: hypothesize, try, measure, refine.

And what we see with the developers we work with is that the winning teams are the ones who move fastest through that loop. They start with a big, capable model to prove out the product idea, because at that stage you just want to know whether it's even possible. Once they find product-market fit, the questions change completely. Now it's about latency, cost, reliability, and quality on *their* specific use case. That's when they start customizing: fine-tuning smaller models on their own data, building compound systems with multiple models and tools working together, and optimizing the whole stack for their workload.

So I'd say the new philosophy is: experiment first, specialize later, and treat your own data and your own feedback loop as the real differentiator. The model alone isn't the product. The product is how well you tailor and orchestrate those models around your users' actual problems. The infrastructure needs to make that iteration cycle as fast and cheap as possible, because speed of iteration is really the competitive advantage now.

r001.rationale: The response calls the model a core building block, but says the model alone is not the product; it does not identify treating the model as a core product asset as a success factor.

r002.rationale: It mentions builders’ own data but does not state that they collect data frontier model labs cannot access.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish frontier labs’ curated data distribution from data generated through application use.

r004.rationale: It does not describe a training-data and application-data mismatch or say that such a mismatch degrades application quality.

r005.rationale: It calls builders’ own data and feedback loop a real differentiator and describes tailoring models to their specific use cases as part of the competitive advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I think the biggest shift is that generative AI is turning application building into a design-first process rather than an infrastructure-first one. In the previous era, if you wanted machine learning in your product, you needed a team of ML engineers, you needed to collect labeled data, train a model, deploy it, and maintain it for months before you ever saw whether users even cared. That meant most product teams never got to experiment with ML at all. With foundation models, a product developer can take an off-the-shelf model, prompt it, and have a working prototype in an afternoon. So the center of gravity moves to the product person and the application developer. The question is no longer "can we build this model?" but "what experience do we want, and how fast can we iterate on it?"

The second thing I'd say is that iteration speed becomes the core competency. These models are non-deterministic, so you can't fully spec out behavior up front. You have to ship, observe how real users interact, and tune. That's very different from traditional software, where you write the logic and it does what you wrote. Here you're shaping behavior through prompts, through retrieval, through fine-tuning on your own data, and the teams that win are the ones who can close that loop quickly. That's actually a big part of why we started Fireworks. We saw a lot of developers getting stuck not on ideas but on the plumbing: latency, cost, model quality, having to stitch together GPUs and inference stacks. If that layer is handled for them, they can spend their time on the product.

And the third shift, which I think people underestimate, is that the product itself becomes a data flywheel. Every interaction generates signal about what users want and where the model falls short. Application builders who treat that as an asset and feed it back into customizing their models end up with something defensible, because the open base models are increasingly commoditized. The differentiation moves up the stack, into the experience and into the proprietary data loop. So the philosophy really becomes: start small with a general model, get to users fast, and then specialize aggressively based on what you learn.

r001.rationale: The response calls user interaction signals and the proprietary data loop an asset, but does not clearly identify the model itself as a core product asset.

r002.rationale: It does not state that application developers collect data frontier model labs cannot access.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish frontier labs’ curated data distribution from data generated through application use.

r004.rationale: It does not describe a training-data and application-data mismatch degrading model quality.

r005.rationale: It says builders can use their own interaction data to customize models and that this proprietary data loop makes their product defensible.

astra-6.text:
I think generative AI changes both what we can build and how we build it. Traditionally, you define the product requirements, translate those into software behavior, and build a fairly predictable experience. With generative AI, you can start with a much more open-ended user need, but the system’s behavior is also less predictable. So evaluation and learning from users become central to product development.

For application builders, that means a compelling demo is really just the beginning. You have to understand where the model works, where it fails, and how those failures affect the user. Then you iterate on the model, the data, and the product experience together.

It also creates an opportunity to rethink the workflow itself. If you’re building a tool to help someone accomplish a task, you can ask: How much of that task can the system now take on? Where does the user need visibility or control? Those questions can lead to very different products from simply adding a chat interface to an existing application.

r001.rationale: The response says builders should iterate on the model, data, and product experience together, but does not identify the model as a core product asset.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning from users but does not state that application developers collect data unavailable to frontier model labs.

r003.rationale: The response does not distinguish frontier labs’ curated data distribution from data generated through application use.

r004.rationale: It discusses model failures generally, but does not connect degraded application quality to a mismatch between training and application data distributions.

r005.rationale: The response mentions iterating on data but does not identify effective use of application-specific data as a competitive advantage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think generative AI changes both what we can build and how we build it. Traditionally, application developers define the behavior pretty explicitly: you have requirements, you write the logic, and you test whether the software follows that logic. With generative AI, you can build experiences around much more open-ended user intent, but the output is also less predictable.

So the product development process becomes much more iterative. You need to understand the user’s task, build a prototype, evaluate it on realistic examples, and learn where the model succeeds or fails. Evaluation and user feedback become part of the development loop from the beginning.

It also pushes builders to rethink the experience itself. Instead of simply adding a chatbot to an existing application, you can ask: What work can the application now do for the user? Where should the user guide it, and where should they review the result? Those decisions become central to the product.
